d: Wilfully obstinate; stubbornly disobedient
ety: From Latin contumāx (“stubborn, obstinate”) + -ious. By surface analysis, contum(ax) + -acious.
s: In all places too are Dissident Priests; whom the Legislative will have to deal with: contumacious individuals, working on that angriest of passions; plotting, enlisting.

d: Having turns or windings
ety: From Latin flexuosus, from flexus (“bend”), from flectere (“bend”).
s: The flexuous bed of the stream.

d: Deserving or inciting pity
ety: From about 1400, from hap (“luck”) + -less.
s: My dear friend, are you to become that hapless kind of outcast, a champion of lost causes?

d: Decoration consisting of an open pattern of interlacing ribs
ety: From trace + -ery.
s: Because of the flamelike undulations of its window tracery, the Norman archæologist, M. de Caumont, who had brought into use the name Romanesque, invented the equally useful term Flamboyant.

d: A platform raised above the surrounding level to give prominence to the person on it
ety: Learned borrowing from Latin rōstrum (“beak, snout”), from rōd(ō) (“gnaw”) + -trum, from Proto-Indo-European *Hreh₃d- + *-trom. The pulpit sense is a back-formation from the name of the Roman Rōstra, the platforms in the Forum where politicians made speeches. The Rōstra were decorated with (and named for) the beaks (prows) of ships from naval victories.
s: He saw a crowd listening to a man who was talking from the rostrum of a kitchen-chair.

d: A long loud emotional utterance
ety: ] Borrowed from Latin ululātiō, from ululō (“to howl, shriek, yell”) (from a reduplicated Proto-Indo-European imitative root) + -ātiō (suffix forming nouns relating to some action or the result of an action) (from Proto-Indo-European *-tis (suffix forming abstract or action nouns from verb roots)). By surface analysis, ululate + -ion.
s: As ululations and celebratory gunfire filled the air, the mood was one of fragile joy.

d: An architectural ornament consisting of a horizontal sculptured band between the architrave and the cornice
ety: Late Middle English, from French and Middle French frise, probably from Medieval Latin Frisia (“Frisian (wool)”) due to import via Northern ships. Or, from French friser (“to curl”)..
s: The classroom had an alphabet frieze that showed an animal for each letter.

d: Overeat or eat immodestly; make a pig of oneself
ety: From French engorger, from Old French engorgier. Archaic spellings from Webster’s dictionary 1913 include ingorge and ingorg, both now considered misspellings.
s: Greedily she engorged without restraint

d: Belonging to some prior time
ety: From erst (“first, formerly”) + while.
s: If you're for one of my erstwhile opponents, that's O.K. Just don't work too hard.

d: Speak to someone
ety: From Middle French accoster, acoster, from Old French acoster (“to stand beside”) (whence Medieval Latin accostare), from Old French a- + coste (“side, flank”).
s: A beggar accosted me as soon as I stepped outside.

d: Portable bulletproof shelter
ety: From Middle English mauntelet, from Old French mantelet, diminutive of mantel (“mantle”). Doublet of mantelletta.
s: Already their archers were stealing forward, pushing their rolling mantlets.

d: Make peace with
ety: From Latin propitiāt-, the past participial stem of propitiāre (“make favourable”), from propitius (“favourable, gracious”).
s: But polite and politic it is, to propitiate your hostess.

d: A pensive lyrical piece of music (especially for the piano)
ety: Borrowed from French nocturne (literally “nocturnal”), from Latin nocturnus. Doublet of notturno.
s: The vocal nocturne, in other words, turns out to be no easier a genre to define than the piano nocturne. But its ambiguities are nevertheless helpful in making sense of those of the piano nocturne.

d: Liveliness and eagerness
ety: Mid-15th century; from Middle English alacrite, from Latin alacritās, from alacer (“brisk”) + -itās (“-ity”).
s: I have not that alacrity of spirit / Nor cheer of mind that I was wont to have.

d: Characterized by an inability to mask your feelings; not devious
ety: Learned borrowing from Latin ingenuus (“of noble character, frank”). Doublet of ingenu.
s: There was nothing more I dared say. My ingenuous attempts to lie my way out of trouble had only served to get me in deeper and deeper.

d: The process of using your mind to consider something carefully
ety: From Latin cerebrum (“brain”) + -ation.
s: Duncan himself, however, seems to have alpine cerebrations embedded in his very molecules.

d: Deadly or sinister
ety: From Middle English baleful, balful, baluful, from Old English bealuful, which was equivalent to bealu + -ful. By surface analysis, bale (“evil, woe”) + -ful. See bale for further etymology.
s: With balefull weedes, and precious Iuiced flowers, / The earth that's Natures mother, is her Tombe,

d: The ambiguity of an individual word or phrase that can be used (in different contexts) to express two or more different meanings
ety: From polyseme + -y.
s: Polysemy proliferates in natural language: Virtually every word is polysemous to some extent.

d: Telling fortunes by lines on the palm of the hand
ety: From Middle English palmestrie. Equivalent to palm + -ist + -ry.
s: Chiromantie is a coniecturyng by beholdyng the lynes, or wryncles of the handes called commonly Palmistry.

d: Pleasing to the ear
ety: From Middle English mellifluous, mellyfluous, from Latin mellifluus (“flowing like honey”) + -ous, from mel (“honey”) + fluō (“flow”). Compare superfluous and fluid, from same root, and with dulcet (“sweet speech”), alternative Latinate term with a similar meaning.
s: Radio proved a perfect fit for the mellifluous tones of Mr. Pence, who called himself “Rush Limbaugh on decaf.”

d: The molding around a door or window
ety: First attested 1563, borrowed from Italian architrave, from archi- (“main”) + trave (“beam”).
s: I know that one hinge of this door has parted with the woodwork. Dry rot has turned the architrave to compacted dust.

d: Lengthen in time; cause to be or last longer
ety: From the past participle stem of Latin prōtrahō. By surface analysis, pro- + tract.
s: A cat can protract and retract its claws.

d: Compare critically; of texts
ety: From Latin collātus, perfect passive participle of conferō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix). Doublet of confer. See also infer, delate and defer (Etymology 2), relate and refer, as well as prelate and prefer among others. Not related to collateral.
s: Collating was still necessary because they had to insert foldout sheets and index tabs into the documents.

d: Deserving of respect or high regard
ety: From Middle English estimable, estymable, from Old French estimable, from Latin aestimābilis. Equivalent to esteem + -able and estimate + -able.
s: After this time boric acid is always present in estimable amounts.

d: A noisy or scolding or domineering woman
ety: Borrowed from Latin virāgō (“warlike or heroic woman”, literally “manlike”).
s: Joan was all Arden, grinning there, siding with her virago mother.

d: A political leader (especially of Tammany Hall)
ety: Borrowed from Narragansett sachem; compare Mi'kmaq saqamaw (“chief”) and Unami sakima (“chief”), all ultimately from Proto-Algonquian *sa·kima·wa. Doublet of sagamore.
s: If a sachem was too harsh, a tribesman might leave and join another tribe.

d: An ancestor in the direct line
ety: From Middle English progenitour, from Anglo-Norman progenitour, Middle French progeniteur (Modern French progéniteur), and their etymon Latin prōgenitor, from prōgenitus, perfect participle of prōgignere (“to beget”), itself from prō- (“forth”) + gignere (“to beget”). By surface analysis, pro- (“prior, fore-”) + genitor.
s: ARPANET was the progenitor of the Internet.

d: Capable of or tending to change in form or quality or nature
ety: From Middle English mutable, from Old French mutable, from Latin mutabilis (“liable to change”). By surface analysis, muta- + -able.
s: It is in vain to interpose the explanation that the sonship was mutable. The Broad School do not say so ; and in so far they are consistent, for they recognise no power to produce the mutation.

d: Excessively unwilling to spend
ety: From parsimony + -ous.
s: Statistical methods offer the ability to enforce parsimonious selection of the most influential potential predictors of each gene's state.

d: A stone coffin (usually bearing sculpture or inscriptions)
ety: The noun is borrowed from Latin sarcophagus (“grave; sarcophagus; flesh-eating, carnivorous”), from Ancient Greek σᾰρκοφᾰ́γος (sărkophắgos, “sarcophagus; flesh-eating, carnivorous”) (so named from λῐ́θος σᾰρκοφᾰ́γος (lĭ́thos sărkophắgos, literally “flesh-eating stone”) a type of limestone found at Assos in Troas (now Behramkale, Turkey) thought to consume the flesh of corpses, and thus used to mak
s: On the lids of those Tombs; square sarcophaguses, in that silent dim-burning Hall, each with its Soul in torment; the lids open there; they are to be shut at the Day of Judgment, through Eternity.

d: The military governor of a frontier province in medieval Germany
ety: From Middle Dutch marcgrāve (modern Dutch markgraaf), cognate with Old High German marcgrāvo (modern German Markgraf), from Proto-Germanic *markō (“boundary; boundary marker”) + *grafa (“military rank”), from Latin graphio. More at mark, graft. Compare marchion, marquis, landgrave.
s: The Margrave of Bruges was their head.

d: An authoritative command or request
ety: From Middle English biheste, from Old English behǣs (“vow, promise”), from Proto-West Germanic *bihaisi, from *bi- (“be-”) + *haisi (“command”), from Proto-Germanic *haisiz, from *haitaną (“to command”). Final -t by analogy with other similar words in -t. Related to Old English behātan (“to command, promise”), Middle Low German beheit, behēt (“a promise”). Compare also hest (“command”), hight.
s: Paul did not dare pronounce, let matters rest, / His master having given him no behest.

d: A large wardrobe or cabinet; originally used for storing weapons
ety: Unadapted borrowing from Middle French armoire. Doublet of ambry, armarium, and almirah.
s: In 2003, at Neal Auction Company in New Orleans, an 1810s mahogany armoire inlaid with ribbons and vines brought $140,000 (the presale estimate was $30,000 to $50,000).

d: A metal cap or band placed on a wooden pole to prevent splitting
ety: From Middle English verel, virel, virole (“ferrule; metal pivot on the end of an axle”), altered under the influence of Latin ferrum (“iron”), from Old French virole (“ferrule”), from Latin viriola (“little bracelet”), diminutive of viria (“bracelet worn by men”), from Gaulish, from Proto-Celtic *weiros (“crooked”) (compare Middle Irish fiar (“bent, crooked”), Welsh gŵyr, Breton gwar (“curved”)),
s: Lucas withdrew the cane. Its polished ferrule flashed in the lantern glare.

d: With wings extended in a flying position
ety: From Middle French volant, present participle of voler (“to fly”), from Latin volāre.
s: A demi-ostrich, wings volant proper.

d: The elementary stages of any subject (usually plural)
ety: From Old French rudiment, from Latin rudimentum (“a first attempt, a beginning”), plural rudimenta (“the elements”), from rudis (“rude”); see rude. By surface analysis, rude + -i- + -ment.
s: I have the rudiments of an escape plan.

d: An incompetent or clumsy person
ety: Cognate with duff, which see (origin is uncertain).
s: Besides, I was anxious to take the wheel, the man in pink pyjamas showing himself a hopeless duffer at the business.

d: A heap of earth placed over prehistoric tombs
ety: From Latin tumulus (“mound, hill”), from tumeō (“to swell”). Doublet of tombolo.
s: They planted the cannon on the tumuli, sole elevations in this level country, and formed themselves into column and hollow square.

d: A total abstainer
ety: From teetotal + -er.
s: The six drivers foregathered and the rather surprising discovery was made that five out of the six were teetotallers.

d: Act of demanding or levying by force or authority
ety: From Middle English exaccioun, exaccion, from Middle French exaction, from Old French, from Latin exāctiō.
s: Exaction of various dues and fees.
